questions.stem: A drug is eliminated by zero-order kinetics with k0 = 10 mg/L per hour, starting at 100 mg/L. How long does it take to fall from 100 to 50 mg/L, and then from 50 to 25 mg/L?
questions.explanation: Zero-order: a constant amount (10 mg/L) is removed each hour, so t½ = 0.5C0/k0: 50/10 = 5 h, then 25/10 = 2.5 h. The half-life shortens as concentration falls. A: A constant half-life is a first-order feature. B: Treats the drug as first-order with a constant half-life; zero-order t½ isn't constant. D: Uses C0/k0 (time to reach zero), not 0.5C0/k0. E: Reverses the trend; zero-order t½ gets shorter, not longer.

questions.stem: A drug follows first-order kinetics with a Vd of 40 L and a clearance of 4 L/h. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL = 0.693 × 40 / 4 ≈ 6.9 h. A: Inverts the ratio (CL/Vd × 0.693). B: Omits 0.693 (Vd/CL only). C: Divides by 0.693 instead of multiplying. D: Multiplies 0.693 by Vd but forgets to divide by CL.

questions.stem: A drug with first-order elimination and a half-life of 8 hours is started as a constant IV infusion without a loading dose. About how long until it reaches 95% of its steady-state concentration?
questions.explanation: 95% of Css takes ~4.32 half-lives → 4.32 × 8 ≈ 35 h. B: One half-life gives 50%. C: Two half-lives give 75%. D: Three half-lives give 87.5%. E: ~6.6 half-lives (53 h) is needed for 99%.

questions.stem: A drug given by IV infusion has a Vd of 50 L and a clearance of 5 L/h. A plasma concentration of 10 mg/L is needed quickly. What loading dose should be given?
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × Ctarget = 50 L × 10 mg/L = 500 mg; clearance sets the maintenance rate, not the loading dose. A: Divides Vd by Ctarget. B: CL × Ctarget is the maintenance infusion rate (50 mg/h). C: Multiplies Vd by CL. E: Overestimates by 10×.

questions.stem: An oral drug (F = 0.5) has a clearance of 2 L/h. The target average steady-state concentration is 15 mg/L, given every 12 hours. What maintenance dose is needed?
questions.explanation: Dose = Css × CL × τ / F = 15 × 2 × 12 / 0.5 = 720 mg. A: Ignores F and halves the result. C: Ignores F (the IV dose). D: Omits the dosing interval. E: Corrects for F twice.

questions.stem: A drug following first-order kinetics is given repeatedly at a dosing interval equal to its half-life. What is the accumulation factor (R)?
questions.explanation: Half of each dose is lost per interval → R = 1 / fraction lost = 1 / 0.5 = 2. A: R ≈ 1 only when the interval is ≥ 5 half-lives. B: R = 1.5 needs a longer interval (~1.6 half-lives). C: R = 3 needs an interval shorter than one half-life. D: Not consistent with dosing every half-life.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with epilepsy has a phenytoin level of 12 mg/L. Her dose is increased by about 15%. Two weeks later she has nystagmus and ataxia, and her level is 28 mg/L. What best explains the disproportionate rise?

options.B: Saturation of the metabolizing enzymes (zero-order kinetics)

questions.explanation: At therapeutic levels phenytoin metabolism nears saturation, so elimination becomes constant-amount (zero-order); small dose increases cause large, unpredictable level jumps. A: Auto-induction would lower levels. C: Vd doesn't change with a small dose increase. D: Bioavailability is already high and doesn't explain non-proportional kinetics. E: Not the mechanism for phenytoin's behavior.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (GFR 25 mL/min) needs a renally cleared drug. Compared with a patient with normal kidneys, how should the loading and maintenance doses be adjusted?

options.A: Loading dose decreased; maintenance dose unchanged
options.D: Loading dose unchanged; maintenance dose decreased
options.E: Loading dose increased; maintenance dose decreased

questions.explanation: Loading dose depends on Vd (unchanged), while maintenance dose depends on clearance (reduced in renal failure). A: Reverses the dependencies. B: Lowering the loading dose would delay reaching target levels. C: Higher maintenance doses would cause accumulation and toxicity. E: There is no reason to raise the loading dose.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe renal impairment receives repeated doses of meperidine for pain. On day 3 he develops tremor and a seizure, although his meperidine level is in the usual range. What best explains this?

options.A: Accumulation of an active, toxic metabolite
options.C: Reduced volume of distribution of meperidine
options.E: Displacement of meperidine from plasma proteins

questions.explanation: In renal impairment the metabolite normeperidine accumulates; its toxicity is not predicted by parent-drug levels. B: Saturation would raise the parent-drug level. C: A smaller Vd would also raise the parent-drug level. D: Tolerance reduces the effect; it doesn't cause seizures. E: Displacement gives only a transient rise in free drug and wouldn't depend on renal function.

questions.stem: After an IV bolus, a drug's log plasma concentration–time plot shows a steep initial fall followed by a slower straight-line decline. What does the steep initial phase mainly represent?

options.C: Distribution of drug from plasma into tissues

questions.explanation: This is the two-compartment model: a biexponential decline made of two first-order processes, distribution (early, steep) then elimination (later, linear). A: Both phases are first-order in this model; zero-order elimination would not give a biexponential curve. B: An IV bolus has no absorption phase. D: First-pass metabolism applies to oral drugs. E: Enterohepatic recirculation causes secondary peaks, not an initial steep fall.
